Issues

1. Remote-code-execution vulnerability  
   • yaml.load() with no Loader argument will happily construct any Python
     object that is encoded in the YAML, e.g.

        !!python/object/apply:os.system ["rm -rf /"]

     If the YAML comes from an untrusted source this is a critical
     security hole (CVE-2017-5951).  
   • In recent PyYAML versions the call you wrote even raises a
     YAMLLoadWarning telling you exactly this.

2. Deprecated / undefined behaviour  
   • Since PyYAML 5.1 the signature without an explicit Loader is
     deprecated.  Future versions may remove it altogether.

3. No error handling  
   • Malformed YAML will raise yaml.YAMLError and bubble up.  The caller
     gets an untyped exception and no context.

4. Import inside the function  
   • Importing on every call is unnecessary overhead and hides import
     errors until runtime.  It also makes the function slower inside
     tight loops.

5. Weak API design  
   • No type hints, no docstring.  
   • The function will return None for an empty string, or a scalar /
     list for a non-mapping root, which may break callers that expect a
     dict.

How to fix

```
from typing import Any, Dict
import yaml

def parse_config(config_str: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Safely parse a YAML configuration string and return a dictionary.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If the YAML is invalid or the root element is not a mapping.
    """
    try:
        data: Any = yaml.safe_load(config_str)          # safe ‑- no code exec
    except yaml.YAMLError as err:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid YAML: {err}") from err

    if data is None:
        return {}                                       # or raise, your call
    if not isinstance(data, dict):
        raise ValueError("Configuration root must be a mapping")

    return data
```

Additional recommendations

• If you need more permissive loading (anchors, aliases, etc.) use  
  yaml.load(config_str, Loader=yaml.FullLoader) rather than the unsafe
  default.

• Consider pinning PyYAML in requirements.txt to avoid surprise
  behaviour changes.

• For tighter safety you can whitelist allowed tags/keys or switch to
  ruamel.yaml which supports round-trip preservation and stricter
  loaders.

• Add unit tests that feed malicious YAML payloads to guarantee the
  loader you chose really stays safe.
